subject: ss-critical-care
title: Tumour lysis syndrome in the critically ill cancer patient

steps.tx: **Tumour lysis syndrome** (TLS) follows rapid release of intracellular contents after cytotoxic therapy kills tumour cells. The release causes **hyperkalaemia**, **hyperphosphataemia**, hypocalcaemia, and **hyperuricaemia**, which can lead to acute kidney injury and arrhythmias. Burkitt lymphoma, high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and acute leukaemia carry the highest risk. Pre-existing renal impairment is an established predisposing factor, as is high tumour proliferation rate and large tumour burden.

steps.tx: Diagnosis of **tumour lysis syndrome** relies on the **Cairo-Bishop** definitions. Laboratory disease requires abnormal levels of uric acid, potassium, phosphate or calcium around the time of cytotoxic treatment, judged against a recent window before and after therapy. Clinical disease adds kidney injury, cardiac rhythm disturbance or seizures. Raised phosphate is typical after chemotherapy, whereas spontaneous breakdown may leave phosphate normal. Dangerous **ventricular arrhythmias** make continuous ECG monitoring essential.

rows: Abnormal uric acid, potassium, phosphate or calcium
Urgent treatment and dialysis if needed

steps.tx: Prevention is the priority. Start **allopurinol** 24 to 48 hours before chemotherapy, or use **rasburicase** when uric acid is high or the patient is at high risk. Rasburicase converts uric acid to allantoin, which is far more soluble. Check G6PD status before rasburicase, because it can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Give hydration with urine output near 2 mL/kg/h. Avoid potassium and calcium in initial fluids, and avoid routine alkalinisation because it promotes calcium-phosphate precipitation.

steps.tx: Beyond TLS, the critically ill cancer patient often has **neutropenic sepsis**, **cytokine release syndrome** after CAR-T therapy, and **haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis** (HLH). HLH is diagnosed by at least five of eight HLH-2004 criteria. Malignancy is the commonest adult trigger, and malignancy-associated HLH carries a much poorer median survival than non-malignant HLH. Differentiation syndrome occurs with arsenic and retinoic acid therapy in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

steps.tx: Set goals early. A **time limited trial** of intensive care is reasonable when the expected outcome is poor, with shared decisions involving the patient and family. Relapsed lymphoma with HLH and multiorgan failure that does not respond to bridging therapy has a poor prognosis, and **haematopoietic stem cell transplant** is the only potentially curative option once stable. Document the review points and the criteria for stopping escalation.
